headline: Forecasting one or two more RBA rate hikes — September and Melbourne Cup Day board meetings — adding ~$7,000 per annum to an average $1M loan
reasoning: Dix highlights that the market is broadly pricing in a September RBA hike and possibly a second hike around Melbourne Cup Day in November. He notes that the cumulative rate rises since COVID have added around $7,000 of additional annual interest payments on an average $1 million loan, which is a real cost to balance sheets. Despite this, the primary RBA concern remains inflation, as signalled by multiple board members speaking publicly in the prior week.
quote: So we're looking at the end of September for the next RBA board meeting and then Melbourne Cup Day. So could well be that we end up with another rate rise on Melbourne Cup Day, which is not something that the community wants to see, but it it they need to, the RBA needs to, needs to be, you know, the pressures of inflation have been ever present since COVID and, and that's their primary concern. So we've seen that over the past week or so with a number of RBA board members come out in the market and talk about the pressures of inflation, hence the reason why interest rates will probably adjust.

headline: Low unemployment (~4.5%) underpins borrower resilience in Australian property loan books
reasoning: Dix points to Australia's unemployment rate of approximately 4.5% as a key macro support factor for property loan performance. He argues this relatively low unemployment rate sustains borrower capacity to service debt, reducing credit risk for lenders operating in the residential and SME commercial property space.
quote: And as I said, the, the resilience of the borrow and I mean unemployment is still very low in the whole scheme of things that are around 4 1/2%. So for, for us, you know as we, we like sticking to that, that line, we've done so for 20 odd years.

sector: Property Debt / Private Credit - Construction & Development
headline: Cautious on high-yield construction/development private credit structures; warns capitalised interest, media-flagged losses, and distribution cuts are key red flags
reasoning: Dix warns that single-asset or development-style private credit structures carry significantly higher risks, including capitalised interest that requires alternative funding to support distributions. Recent media coverage highlights a flight of capital toward high-yielding assets in this space. While not all operators will suffer significant losses if structured correctly, distribution adjustments to investors are a warning sign warranting further questions to the manager. Budget tax changes may also force some operators in this niche to find different markets.
quote: Yes, there's certainly been a flight of capital towards high yielding assets and I think the market environment has been quite good for those providers. Even though there's a lot of media interest in this space, it doesn't mean that there will be significant losses to the private credit operators. Some may well have some losses, but if they're structured things right, there should be a return of capital or maybe a a marginal loss perhaps where the, the, I guess losses will be seen is more in the distribution. So what return is being provided to investors on a monthly basis may have to adjust. So that's probably, you know, the, the main I guess warning sign at the moment is a is a change of distribution to investors. It probably warrants a few more questions to the manager.

headline: Australian property debt market is resilient with very low arrears across residential and commercial books, despite 13+ rate rises post-COVID and ongoing inflation pressure
reasoning: David Dix notes that arrears rates across Thinktank's residential and commercial book remain very low despite around 13 interest rate rises post-COVID, a couple of cuts, and then a further 75 basis points of additional cost in early 2025. He acknowledges some cracks at the margins in the Victorian market and pressure from higher-for-longer rates but says overall the book is robust. He flags that another one or two RBA rate rises are possible (September and Melbourne Cup Day board meetings), which would add further cost to borrowers but does not expect material stress given adaptation so far.
quote: I think the property market is, it is essentially working and working well. I mean, the market that we operate in is both residential and commercial property. It's at the, I would say the smaller end of the spectrum. So we're talking about, you know, loan sizes of generally around $1,000,000, maybe a little bit less, maybe a little bit more depending on the assets. And I think we're in a, the Australian economy is, is relatively robust. I think we're seeing some cracks at the margins, certainly around where interest rates are AT and perhaps inflation. But across the board we're seeing very low arrears rates across our book, both residential and commercial.

headline: Positive on the residential and commercial property debt space targeting mum-and-dad borrowers, avoiding construction/development finance; sustainability of returns over high double-digit yields
reasoning: David Dix argues that the key to managing risk in property private credit is diversity across residential and commercial loans and avoiding construction/development finance. He emphasises that conservative, sustainable returns are preferable to chasing double-digit yields that require taking on riskier credit. He notes that unemployment around 4.5% supports borrower resilience. Institutional markets (domestic banks investing in RMBS and CMBS) are comfortable with this space, validating the asset class. Thinktank has maintained this lane for 20+ years and does not do construction development finance.
quote: Well, I would say we're positive on the space that we operate in certainly. So it's the smaller end of town. It's, it's more of the mum and dad type borrowers. And as I said, the, the resilience of the borrow and I mean unemployment is still very low in the whole scheme of things that are around 4 1/2%. So for, for us, you know as we, we like sticking to that, that line, we've done so for 20 odd years. We don't do construction development finance. It's not just not part of I guess where we've come from and who we are. So for us, sustainability of returns becomes really important.

headline: RMBS and CMBS default rates have historically been very low, making the sector attractive to institutional investors; macroeconomic risk is the primary concern rather than structural credit risk
reasoning: Dix explains that institutional investors are attracted to the RMBS and CMBS space because historical default rates have been very low. He manages around $10 billion of assets for institutions in this segment. He argues that the key risk is macroeconomic — inflation and interest rates affecting borrowers' ability to pay — rather than structural issues, given conservative LTV ratios and portfolio diversification across approximately 15,000 loans. He also warns self-directed investors to scrutinise single-asset and development-style private credit structures carefully, particularly around capitalised interest arrangements.
quote: I guess for us, what people are getting exposed to is a very diversified set of loans. So that's really important. It's part of the reason why we manage around $10 billion of assets for institutions. The institutions really like the space that we operate in because the I guess the default rates across RMBS and CMBS markets, so residential and commercial mortgage backed securities has been very low in history. So depending on where they sit in the capital structure that's really important as well. But I would say risk reward, it's it's been a very important market and one that we participate in and are very comfortable with the risk and return profile.
